explanations.answer: Back to every town where they preached
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul, the traveling teacher, tells Barnabas, his partner in the work, “Let us go back and visit the brothers in every town where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.” That's a check-in tour. I think Paul wanted to see the faces behind the word he'd preached. (Acts 15:36)

explanations.answer: Up to Jerusalem for another meeting
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but that's not Paul's plan. Jerusalem does come up in this passage, because the decisions of the apostles and elders came from there (Acts 16:4). But Paul's idea in verse 36 is to go back and visit the brothers in every town where they proclaimed the word. Nobody schedules a meeting here. It's a visit, and I'd bring dough.

explanations.answer: Down to Egypt to start somewhere new
explanations.explanation: Egypt is a long walk from this verse, baker. Paul isn't starting somewhere new at all. He says, “Let us go back and visit the brothers in every town where we proclaimed the word of the Lord…” (Acts 15:36). It's a return trip to visit the brothers in those towns, and Egypt isn't mentioned anywhere.

The text gives that reason, baker. It says Paul thought it best not to take Mark, John also called Mark, “…because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work.” That's the writer telling us why. I think it was a hard thing for both men to sit across from. (Acts 15:38)

Nope, nothing about elders in this argument. The text names one reason: Mark “…had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work.” Mark isn't said to have argued with anybody. Sometimes the real reason is on the page and we go hunting for a juicier one. (Acts 15:38)

explanations.answer: Mark wanted to stay in Antioch
explanations.explanation: Mark's own wishes aren't mentioned here, friend. The text says Barnabas wanted to take him, and Paul thought it best not to, “…because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work.” That's the reason on the page. Anything about Mark wanting to stay home would be me making up a story, and I've got enough cookie dough to make up already. (Acts 15:37-38)

I know it'd be nice if they shook hands and kept going, baker. But the text says the opposite. “Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.” These two had traveled together and still couldn't settle it. (Acts 15:39)

That's right, baker. The text says, “Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.” No compromise and no coin flip is mentioned. I think that one stings, because they'd done so much together. (Acts 15:39)

That's the one, baker. “Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus…” Barnabas wanted to take Mark, and this verse shows him doing it. Paul went a different direction, since they parted company. (Acts 15:37, 39)
Crete is an island, so you were thinking in the right direction. But the text says Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus. Cyprus is the island in verse 39. (Acts 15:39)

Malta is an island too, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The text says, “Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus…” Barnabas took Mark along and set sail. Cyprus is the place the verse names, and Malta never comes up. (Acts 15:39)

You got it, baker. Paul “…traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.” He's building people up, and Silas, the one Paul chose, is with him. That's a good way to spend a road trip. (Acts 15:40-41)

Paul isn't scolding anybody in this verse, friend. The text says he traveled through Syria and Cilicia, “…strengthening the churches.” That's encouragement, and no one is getting a finger wagged at them. (Acts 15:41)

Warnings are in the Bible, but they're not what this verse says. Paul traveled through Syria and Cilicia, “…strengthening the churches.” The verse names strengthening, so that's the word that fits. (Acts 15:41)

That's right, baker. Timothy, a disciple Paul found in Lystra, had a good name. “The brothers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.” Two towns spoke well of him, and I'd love to get that review on my cookies. (Acts 16:2)
Not this time, friend. The text says Timothy, a disciple in Lystra, had a good name: “The brothers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.” Two towns, same good word about him. (Acts 16:2)
Paul does the opposite, baker. The text says, “Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, so he took him…” Nobody gets left behind here. Timothy is invited and goes along. (Acts 16:3)

That's right, baker. “Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, so he took him…” Paul found a disciple the brothers spoke well of and brought him along. I think Timothy had a lot of road ahead of him. (Acts 16:2-3)

explanations.answer: The Jews there knew his father was Greek
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul circumcised Timothy “…on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.” Timothy's mother was a believing Jewish woman, and the Jews in that area all knew his father was Greek. That is the reason the text gives. (Acts 16:1, 3)

explanations.answer: The Jerusalem letter said he had to
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason, friend. Paul circumcised Timothy “…on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.” The Jerusalem decisions show up in the very next verse, when the team delivers them from town to town. Verse 3 doesn't connect the two, so I won't either. (Acts 16:3-4)

explanations.answer: Timothy asked Paul to do it first
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says Timothy asked, baker. It says Paul wanted Timothy along, so he took him and circumcised him “…on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.” That's the reason on the page. Anything else would be me adding to the story. (Acts 16:3)

explanations.answer: They grow in numbers every day
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. “So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.” Strong in faith, bigger in numbers, and it kept going day after day. That's a full cookie jar. (Acts 16:5)

explanations.answer: They choose new elders in each town
explanations.explanation: Elders do show up in this passage, friend, but they're in Jerusalem, where the decisions came from (Acts 16:4). The text doesn't say the towns picked new ones. What it says is that the churches “…were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.” Stick with what the verse gives you. (Acts 16:5)

explanations.answer: They send gifts back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Nobody's mailing gifts in this verse, baker. The decisions travel from Jerusalem out to the towns, not the other way around (Acts 16:4). The result is that the churches “…were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.” That's the whole report, and it's a good one. (Acts 16:5)
The door stays shut, baker. The text says, “…they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them.” Paul's team came right up to the border and got a no. (Acts 16:7)

That's right, baker. They tried to enter Bithynia, “…but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them.” It's the second no in a row, since the Holy Spirit had already kept them from speaking the word in Asia. So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. (Acts 16:6-8)

You got it, baker. The text says, “During the night, Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him…” I think a plea like that gets your attention faster than a smoking oven. His words are “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” (Acts 16:9)
Galilee isn't in this vision, friend. Paul saw “…a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him…” Macedonia is where the man is from, and it's where he's asking Paul to come. (Acts 16:9)
Egypt is a long way off, baker, and not in this vision. The text says Paul saw “…a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him…” Same Paul, same night, different map. (Acts 16:9)
That's it, baker. The man says, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” It's a short plea and a clear one. (Acts 16:9)
Timothy is on the team, but the man doesn't ask for him. The plea is, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” He's asking Paul to come, and nobody else is named. (Acts 16:9)

explanations.answer: Pray for their king from Troas
explanations.explanation: The man doesn't mention a king, and he isn't asking for prayers from far away, friend. He pleads, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” He wants Paul to come over to where he is. Troas isn't the plan. (Acts 16:9)
That's right, baker. “As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we got ready to leave for Macedonia…” There's no long delay in the text, and they get ready right then. Nobody hits snooze. (Acts 16:10)

The text says otherwise, friend. “As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we got ready to leave for Macedonia…” They got ready as soon as he saw it. I'd have still been looking for my apron. (Acts 16:10)

explanations.answer: God has called them to preach there
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. As soon as Paul had seen the vision, they got ready to leave for Macedonia, “…concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.” They concluded it was God's call. The text says it plainly. (Acts 16:9-10)

Silas is on the team, but no family is mentioned in this passage, friend. The text says they were “…concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.” That's the whole reason they go. (Acts 16:10)

explanations.answer: The church in Troas sent them
explanations.explanation: Nobody in Troas is said to send them, baker. They got ready to leave “…concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.” The call they name is God's, not a church's. (Acts 16:10)
